A machine-learning project in credit risk

Credit Card Default Risk

We estimate, for each of 30,000 credit-card clients, the probability of defaulting next month, compare five models with a baseline that ignores the client, and turn the probabilities into decisions that treat a missed default as the costlier error.

01 The question

A bank needs a probability, and then a decision

Can we tell, from six months of history, which credit-card clients will fail to pay next month?

A default here means that a client does not make the required payment in the following month. We want a model that gives each client an estimated probability of default, not just a yes or no, because a probability can be ranked, compared and turned into a decision in more than one way.

The project has three parts:

  • Estimate each client's probability of default next month.
  • Compare five models with a baseline that ignores every client characteristic and gives everyone the same probability. A model is useful only if it beats this baseline.
  • Decide: turn probabilities into "flag" or "do not flag", knowing that the two possible errors do not cost the same. A false negative is a missed default: the loan is not repaid. A false positive is a false alarm: a good client is refused or checked for nothing. In credit, a missed default usually costs more.

Takeaway

The goal is a well-judged probability for every client, measured against a baseline, and a decision rule that leans towards catching defaults.

02 The data

Thirty thousand clients, one month to predict

A public dataset of a Taiwanese bank's card holders, clean, but with far more good payers than defaulters.

We use the "Default of Credit Card Clients" dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository: 30,000 clients of a bank in Taiwan, observed from April to September 2005. Each row is one client. The target is 1 if the client defaults in October 2005 and 0 otherwise.

What the columns mean
ColumnMeaning
LIMIT_BALCredit granted, in New Taiwan dollars (NT$)
SEX1 = male, 2 = female
EDUCATION1 = graduate school, 2 = university, 3 = high school, 4 = other (undocumented codes 0, 5, 6 also appear)
MARRIAGE1 = married, 2 = single, 3 = other (code 0 also appears)
AGEAge in years
PAY_0, PAY_2 … PAY_6Repayment status: −1 = paid on time, 1–9 = months of delay (codes −2 and 0 also appear)
BILL_AMT1 … BILL_AMT6Amount on the monthly statement (NT$)
PAY_AMT1 … PAY_AMT6Amount paid (NT$)
Target1 = default in October 2005, 0 = no default

The suffix is the month: 0 or 1 = September 2005 (the most recent), 6 = April 2005. There is no PAY_1. The client ID is not used as an input.

The data are clean: 0 missing values and 0 duplicate client IDs. They are, however, imbalanced: only 6,636 of 30,000 clients default.

No default: 23,364 (77.88%) Default: 6,636 (22.12%)

This imbalance sets the bar. A "model" that always answers no default is right for every client who pays, so its accuracy (the share of correct answers) is already 77.88%. That is the number to beat, and it is also a warning: a high accuracy alone says little when one class is rare, because the trivial rule catches no defaults at all.

Takeaway

Clean data, 22.12% defaults. Always predicting "no default" scores 77.88% accuracy, so every model must clear that line, and accuracy alone is not enough to judge it.

03 Preparing the variables

Codes become quantities the models can use

Some columns are labels and some mix categories with numbers; we rewrite them so that every input means what it says.

Months of delay

The repayment status PAY_k mixes two kinds of information: the codes −2, −1 and 0 describe ways of paying without delay, while 1 to 9 count months of delay. We keep the quantity that matters, the months of delay:

DELAY_k = max(PAY_k, 0), so all codes that do not indicate a delay become 0.

Labels become 0/1 indicators

SEX, EDUCATION and MARRIAGE are labels, not amounts: "3" for high school is not three times "1" for graduate school. Each becomes a set of 0/1 indicators, one per category except a reference category (male, graduate school, married). The undocumented codes are grouped with "other" (education codes 0, 4, 5, 6; marriage codes 0 and 3). The six indicators are:

  • SEX_FEMALE
  • EDUCATION_UNIVERSITY
  • EDUCATION_HIGH_SCHOOL
  • EDUCATION_OTHER
  • MARRIAGE_SINGLE
  • MARRIAGE_OTHER

Why this can happen before the split

These are row-by-row rewrites fixed by the dataset's documentation. Nothing is estimated from the data, and no client's values depend on any other client, so they can safely be applied before the data are divided into sets.

Takeaway

Repayment codes become months of delay; categories become 0/1 indicators with odd codes grouped as "other". No information leaks between clients.

04 Three sets, three jobs

Fit on one set, choose on another, check on a third

Each set has a single job, so that the final check is made on clients the project has never used for any decision.

All clients are observed over the same months, so the split is random: first 20% of the clients go to the test set, then 25% of the rest go to the validation set. The result is 60 / 20 / 20, with a fixed random seed.

Training 18,000 clients 3,982 defaults (22.12%) Fits the models: weights, trees, scaling statistics.
Validation 6,000 clients 1,327 defaults (22.12%) Makes every choice: settings, final model, thresholds.
Test 6,000 clients 1,327 defaults (22.12%) Used once, at the end, to measure performance.

The split is stratified: each set keeps the same default rate, 22.12%. Stratification uses the label only to balance the proportions of defaulters across the sets. It tells the models nothing about any individual client, and it gives every set the same baseline, so that comparisons between training, validation and test are fair.

Takeaway

18,000 clients to learn from, 6,000 to choose with, 6,000 kept aside for one final measurement, all with the same 22.12% default rate.

05 Features and scaling

Twenty inputs, each on a comparable scale

We drop variables that repeat each other and put the rest on a common scale, using statistics from the training set only.

We measure the Pearson correlation between the 20 quantitative variables (LIMIT_BAL, AGE, six BILL_AMT, six PAY_AMT, six DELAY) on the training set only. A correlation of at least 0.70 in absolute value means that two variables carry almost the same information.

17 pairs reach the threshold, all positive. The six BILL_AMT variables are strongly linked (from 0.951 for BILL_AMT1–BILL_AMT2 to 0.799 for BILL_AMT1–BILL_AMT6), and DELAY_5 is linked to DELAY_4 (0.746) and to DELAY_6 (0.733).

Removal rule. Pairs are examined from the highest correlation to the lowest; if both variables are still present, the one from the older month is dropped, because the recent one is closer to the month being predicted. Only BILL_AMT1 survives among the statements; DELAY_5 leaves in its pair with DELAY_4, which also removes the DELAY_5–DELAY_6 pair.

Removed: BILL_AMT2, BILL_AMT3, BILL_AMT4, BILL_AMT5, BILL_AMT6, DELAY_5. That leaves 14 quantitative variables and 6 indicators, 20 features in all; the largest remaining absolute correlation is 0.687.

  • LIMIT_BAL
  • AGE
  • BILL_AMT1
  • PAY_AMT1
  • PAY_AMT2
  • PAY_AMT3
  • PAY_AMT4
  • PAY_AMT5
  • PAY_AMT6
  • DELAY_0
  • DELAY_2
  • DELAY_3
  • DELAY_4
  • DELAY_6
  • SEX_FEMALE
  • EDUCATION_UNIVERSITY
  • EDUCATION_HIGH_SCHOOL
  • EDUCATION_OTHER
  • MARRIAGE_SINGLE
  • MARRIAGE_OTHER

Scaling

The amounts paid, PAY_AMT, are never negative and very skewed: many zeros and a few huge payments. We first apply log(1 + x), which is defined at zero and compresses the large values. Then every quantitative variable is turned into a z-score, (x − mean) / standard deviation, so that all inputs share one scale. The mean and standard deviation come from the training set only and are reused unchanged for validation and test, so no information from those sets enters the model. The 0/1 indicators are left as they are.

Takeaway

6 redundant variables out, 20 features in. Skewed payments are log-transformed and all quantities standardised with training-set statistics only.

06 Five models against a baseline

Every model beats the baseline; the best are close

Each model is tuned on the validation set, and the final model is the one with the lowest validation loss.

Three ways to score a model

Cross-entropy loss no threshold
The average penalty for the probability given to what actually happened. It rewards well-judged probabilities: saying 90% for a client who then defaults costs little, saying 5% costs a lot. Lower is better.
ROC-AUC no threshold
The probability that a randomly chosen defaulter receives a higher estimated risk than a randomly chosen non-defaulter. It measures how well clients are ranked: 0.5 is a random order, 1 is perfect.
Accuracy, precision, recall need a threshold
These count right and wrong decisions, so a client must first be flagged when the probability reaches a threshold (0.50 until chapter 07). Accuracy is the share of correct answers; precision and recall are defined in chapter 07.

The baseline gives every client the same probability, the default rate of the training set (0.2212). At threshold 0.50 it predicts "no default" for everyone. On the validation set its loss is 0.5284 and its accuracy 0.7788.

Logistic regression

A weighted sum of the features passed through the sigmoid, 1 / (1 + e−z), which turns any number into a probability. It is a neural network with no hidden layers, built in Keras.

Trained with the Adam optimiser on the cross-entropy loss, mini-batches of 32 and at most 200 epochs. Early stopping halts training after 10 epochs without improvement in validation loss and restores the best weights.

Validation loss 0.4477, best epoch 14.

Neural network

Hidden layers with the ReLU function, max(0, z), let the model capture non-linear effects. Three sizes were compared, with the same training set-up as the logistic regression: small (16 neurons), medium (32 and 16) and large (64 and 32, with dropout 0.3: during training 30% of each hidden layer is switched off at random, to limit overfitting).

Validation loss falls as the network grows: 0.4362 (small), 0.4339 (medium), 0.4327 (large). Chosen: the Large network. The gain over logistic regression (0.4477) is modest.

Random Forest Final model

A decision tree splits clients with successive questions on one feature at a time; a leaf's probability is the default rate of the training clients that end up in it. The forest averages 500 trees, each built on a random sample of clients and, at every split, a random subset of features.

We compare the minimum number of clients per leaf (1, 5, 20, 50). Tiny leaves let a tree memorise the training set; larger leaves give smoother probabilities.

With one-client leaves the forest learns the training set almost by heart (training loss 0.1119, training accuracy 0.9997) and has the worst validation loss (0.4339). Validation loss improves up to 20 clients per leaf (0.4259) and rises again at 50 (0.4286). Chosen: 20.

Gradient Boosting

Trees are added one at a time, each correcting the errors of the sum of the previous ones, with a step size (learning rate) of 0.05. The number of trees plays the role of epochs: we keep the number at which validation loss is lowest. We also compare 4, 8 and 16 leaves per tree. Scikit-learn's own early stopping is switched off, since it would hold out its own sample.

The three minima are very close: 0.4307 (4 leaves, 480 trees), 0.4299 (8 leaves, 112 trees), 0.4291 (16 leaves, 111 trees). Chosen: 16 leaves and 111 trees.

All five models beat the baseline: validation loss between 0.4259 and 0.4477 against 0.5284, accuracy between 0.8173 and 0.8218 against 0.7788. The Random Forest has the lowest validation loss (0.4259) and also the highest ROC-AUC (0.7861), so it becomes the final model. On the training set the Random Forest looks much better than the others only because it has already seen those clients; the validation columns are the ones that count.

Takeaway

Every model clears the baseline. The Random Forest (500 trees, at least 20 clients per leaf) wins on validation loss and is the final model, but its lead over the other non-linear models is a few thousandths.

07 From a probability to a decision

The threshold decides which mistakes we make

A probability becomes a decision when we pick a threshold; lowering it catches more defaults at the price of more false alarms.

A client is flagged as a likely default when the estimated probability is at least the threshold t. Nothing makes 0.50 automatically right: the classes are imbalanced and the two errors have different costs. With default as the positive class:

  • Precision = caught defaults / all flagged clients: of the clients we flag, the share who really default.
  • Recall = caught defaults / all defaulters: the share of defaults we catch.

For each model we try every threshold from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.01 (91 values) on the validation set and pick two:

  1. Maximum-accuracy threshold: the one with the highest accuracy (on a tie, the lowest).
  2. Prudent threshold: among thresholds whose accuracy is at most 2 points below the best and whose precision is at least 0.50 (at least one flagged client in two really defaults), the one with the fewest missed defaults (on a tie, the highest).

The two tolerances, 2 accuracy points and precision 0.50, are design choices, not results; the sensitivity table below shows what changes if they move.

Random Forest on the validation set at three thresholds
RuleThresholdAccuracyPrecisionRecallFalse alarms (FP)Missed defaults (FN)
Threshold 0.500.500.82180.68910.3542212857
Maximum-accuracy threshold0.490.82270.68650.3647221843
Prudent threshold0.310.80470.56100.5373558614

For the Random Forest the maximum-accuracy threshold (0.49) changes little compared with 0.50: accuracy 0.8227 against 0.8218. The prudent threshold 0.31 cuts missed defaults from 843 to 614 and lifts recall from 0.3647 to 0.5373. In exchange, false alarms rise from 221 to 558, precision falls to 0.5610 and accuracy to 0.8047, still above the baseline (0.7788).

The baseline has no threshold to choose and stays at 0.50.

Maximum-accuracy thresholds stay close to 0.50 (from 0.42 to 0.50). Prudent thresholds are lower, from 0.30 to 0.32 for every model: a client is flagged once the estimated risk is around 30%.

What the prudent threshold implies about costs

If the probabilities are reliable, a threshold t is the right one when a missed default costs (1 − t) / t times a false alarm. For t = 0.31 the ratio is 2.23. In credit a missed default usually costs more than a good client flagged by mistake, which is why the prudent threshold is the operating one.

How much the tolerance matters

The table repeats the choice of the prudent threshold for the Random Forest, allowing from 0 to 4 accuracy points below the best, with the precision constraint unchanged.

08 What the model looks at

Recent payment delays drive the predictions

Shuffling one feature at a time shows how much the Random Forest relies on it.

Permutation importance: on the validation set we shuffle the values of one feature across clients, which breaks its link with the outcome, and measure how much the validation loss rises (average of 5 shuffles). The more it rises, the more the model depends on that feature.

By far the most important feature is DELAY_0, the months of delay in September: shuffling it raises the validation loss by 0.0633, against 0.0131 for DELAY_2, 0.0101 for LIMIT_BAL and 0.0066 for BILL_AMT1. Sex, education and marital status matter very little (at most 0.0007).

The logistic regression's weights tell a consistent story. Because the quantitative features are standardised, their weights are comparable: DELAY_0 has the largest positive weight among them (0.6760: more delay, more risk), and LIMIT_BAL a negative one (-0.3050: other things equal, a higher credit limit goes with lower risk). EDUCATION_OTHER has the largest weight in absolute value (-1.0700), but it concerns a rare category, and the Random Forest hardly uses it (0.0001).

Takeaway

The useful information sits mostly in recent payment delays, DELAY_0 above all. Demographic indicators add almost nothing.

09 The final check on unseen clients

On new clients the final model holds up

Every choice is now fixed. The test set measures how the chosen model performs on 6,000 clients it has never seen.

For study purposes all five models are evaluated on the test set, so that their behaviour can be compared across training, validation and test. The performance estimate of the project, however, is the final model's: the Random Forest with the thresholds chosen on validation. The comparison on test is not used for any decision.

At the prudent threshold the metrics carry over from validation to test almost unchanged: for the Random Forest, recall 0.5373 and 0.5343, precision 0.5610 and 0.5500. Are the probabilities believable?

If the probabilities are reliable, then among clients with an estimated risk around some value the observed default rate should be close to that value. We split the test clients into five bands of estimated probability, fixed in advance.

Risk bands on the test set (Random Forest)
Estimated probability bandClientsMean predicted riskObserved default rate
0–10%1,6170.06800.0643
10–20%2,2740.14450.1495
20–30%7730.23990.2070
30–50%6330.38250.4028
50–100%7030.65430.6657

The observed rate rises with the band, from 0.0643 to 0.6657, and stays close to the mean predicted risk; the largest gap is in the 20–30% band (0.2399 predicted, 0.2070 observed). The Random Forest's probabilities can therefore be read as risks, not only as scores for ranking clients.

Takeaway

On unseen clients the Random Forest keeps its validation behaviour: loss 0.4321 against 0.5284, ROC-AUC 0.7738, and at the prudent threshold it catches 53.4% of defaults with accuracy 0.8003. Its probabilities match observed default rates band by band.

10 What we can and cannot claim

A consistent gain over the baseline, with clear limits

The results are consistent from validation to test; the limits come from the data, the single split and unknown error costs.

Results

  • All five models beat the baseline on validation and test, in loss and in accuracy. Among the four non-linear models the differences are a few thousandths; logistic regression is slightly behind.
  • The final model, chosen on validation, is the Random Forest with at least 20 clients per leaf: on test, cross-entropy 0.4321 against 0.5284 for the baseline, ROC-AUC 0.7738.
  • At the maximum-accuracy threshold (0.49) test accuracy is 0.8170 against 0.7788, but recall is only 0.3587: two defaults in three slip through.
  • At the prudent threshold (0.31) test recall rises to 0.5343 and missed defaults fall from 851 to 618; precision is 0.5500 and accuracy 0.8003.
  • Estimated probabilities are close to observed default rates in every risk band.
  • The useful information lies mainly in recent payment delays, DELAY_0 in particular.

Limits

  • Sample and period. One bank in Taiwan, one period (2005), a one-month horizon. In another portfolio or another economic cycle the probabilities would have to be re-estimated.
  • Validation. A single random split, no cross-validation: choices made on the validation set depend partly on those 6,000 clients.
  • Hyperparameters. Small grids: three networks, four leaf sizes for the forest, three leaf counts for Gradient Boosting.
  • Error costs. The real costs of false alarms and missed defaults are unknown; the prudent threshold is a design rule, not the result of a cost calculation.
  • Margin over the baseline. The features explain only part of client behaviour, so the gain over the baseline is moderate, and even at the prudent threshold some defaults go undetected.

A note on method: the use of the test set

Here all five models were evaluated on the test set for study purposes, to compare their behaviour across training, validation and test. In a real application the procedure would differ: compare on validation, choose the model with the lowest validation loss (here the Random Forest, with the prudent threshold 0.31), and evaluate only that model, once, on the test set. The performance estimate is therefore the Random Forest's (accuracy 0.8003, recall 0.5343, 618 missed defaults on test); the other four models serve only for comparison.

On test, Gradient Boosting is marginally ahead in loss (0.4309 against 0.4321), in ROC-AUC (0.7780 against 0.7738) and, at the prudent threshold, in accuracy (0.8013 against 0.8003, but with 653 missed defaults against 618). Choosing it now would mean using the test set for a decision and would make the performance estimate optimistic. Differences of a few thousandths are within sampling variability: on validation the Random Forest was ahead, both in loss (the selection criterion) and in ROC-AUC.

Takeaway

The model is a clear improvement over the baseline, and its probabilities can be read as risks. Its estimate rests on one untouched test set, and the threshold encodes a cost judgement that a real lender would need to set with real numbers.

About this project

Authors. Simone Nardi (opens in a new tab) and Thomas Petrera (opens in a new tab).

Tools. Python with pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, TensorFlow/Keras, matplotlib and seaborn. All random seeds are fixed at 42, so the results are reproducible. The full code is in the Jupyter notebook in this repository.

Data. Yeh, I-C. (2009). Default of Credit Card Clients [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C55S3H. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.

Yeh, I-C., & Lien, C-H. (2009). The comparisons of data mining techniques for the predictive accuracy of probability of default of credit card clients. Expert Systems with Applications, 36(2), 2473–2480.
